summary: Maria appreciates Duolingo's flexibility and gamified approach to English learning, which fits smoothly into her busy life as a mom.
top_quotes: Duolingo is like my little escape, you know, when I have a few minutes to myself.
I love that I can pick up my phone and practice English anywhere, anytime—it's flexible, just what I need!
Sometimes, it feels like a game, and I forget I'm actually learning, which is brilliant!

interview_script.question: Intro greeting
interview_script.answer: Oi! Hello, I’m Maria, it’s nice to meet you! How are you today?

interview_script.question: Short version of your life story?
interview_script.answer: Well, I was born and raised in Brazil, in a small city near São Paulo. I’ve always been curious about learning new things, including languages, but life got busy, you know? I got married, and now I have two beautiful kids. A few years ago, we moved to Miami, and, um, adapting to life here has been a journey in itself. I wanted to improve my English, so I could feel more confident in daily interactions. That's when I discovered Duolingo, and it’s been a great companion in my language learning journey.

interview_script.question: Where did you grow up?
interview_script.answer: I grew up in Brazil, in a place called Campinas. It’s a lovely city, not too big, not too small, and close enough to São Paulo for those big city adventures!

interview_script.question: What was it like growing up there?
interview_script.answer: Oh, it was nice, you know? We had our community, family gatherings were big, and always full of food and music. I miss those times, especially the Sunday lunches at my grandma’s house. Life was simple and, um, filled with little joys.

interview_script.question: One turning point in your life?
interview_script.answer: Moving to Miami was definitely, um, a turning point for me. Uprooting my family and starting over in a new country, a new culture, it was... challenging. But it was also exciting. It gave me, and my family, the chance to grow and experience so much more. And, of course, it pushed me to learn English more seriously.

interview_script.question: Why was that a turning point?
interview_script.answer: It forced me out of my comfort zone, you know? I had to adapt to a new environment, learn a new language, meet new people. Everything was different—from how you shop for groceries to how you talk to your neighbors. It was a whole new way of life.

interview_script.question: How did you handle that situation?
interview_script.answer: In the beginning, it was, um, overwhelming. But I took it one step at a time. I focused on learning English through Duolingo, watched a lot of English TV shows, and tried to practice speaking whenever I could. I also kept close contact with friends back home, which helped me feel connected. Slowly, I started to feel more at home here.

interview_script.question: What do you care most about right now?
interview_script.answer: Oh, definitely my family. Making sure my kids are adjusting well and that they’re happy is my top priority. Also, I care a lot about improving my English skills because it helps me in everyday life and makes me feel more confident in this new place.

interview_script.question: Why is that important?
interview_script.answer: Well, family is everything, right? Their happiness affects everything. And speaking English well, it's like... it opens doors, you know? It means being able to communicate, connect, and not feel like an outsider. Plus, it sets a good example for my kids.

interview_script.question: What is a good day for you?
interview_script.answer: Ah, a good day is when we spend time together as a family, maybe a picnic at the park, and I feel like I learned something new. Also, if I manage to squeeze in some Duolingo practice, I feel really accomplished. And, of course, if the kids go to bed without a fuss, that’s a win!

interview_script.question: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
interview_script.answer: It’s the little moments, you know? Like when I can have a meaningful conversation in English without feeling lost, or when my son tells me a new English word he learned at school. Those moments make the day feel rewarding.

interview_script.question: How do you make big decisions?
interview_script.answer: Well, I tend to think a lot, maybe too much sometimes. I talk to my husband, weigh the pros and cons, and then, um, I trust my gut feelings. I pray too, ask for guidance, you know, just to make sure I’m doing the right thing for my family.

interview_script.question: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
interview_script.answer: I’d say I’m a bit of both. I like to plan, especially with kids, because routine helps us all. But sometimes, I just, you know, go with the flow when things don’t go as planned. Flexibility is key with kids!

interview_script.question: Example showing that?
interview_script.answer: Last week, we planned a beach day, and then it started raining. Instead of getting upset, we just turned it into a movie day at home. I cooked some Brazilian snacks, and we watched 'Finding Nemo', which the kids loved. It turned out to be a fun day!

interview_script.question: How do you handle risk?
interview_script.answer: Oh, I’m cautious by nature. But moving to Miami taught me that sometimes you have to take risks for greater rewards. I try to evaluate the situation, you know, and if the potential benefits outweigh the risks, then I go for it. I think it’s all about finding the balance.

interview_script.question: Typical weekday?
interview_script.answer: My weekdays are pretty, um, busy. I wake up early, get the kids ready for school. After they leave, I catch up on house chores, do some grocery shopping. Then, I usually have some time for myself, that’s when I do Duolingo. I pick up the kids in the afternoon, help with homework, and we usually spend some quality time until dinner. Evenings can be a mix of family time and preparing for the next day.

interview_script.question: Which parts take the most energy?
interview_script.answer: Definitely the mornings, getting the kids up and ready, and the late afternoons when they need attention and help with their schoolwork. It’s non-stop energy, you know, trying to keep up with their boundless energy!

interview_script.question: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
interview_script.answer: Oh, I wish I had more time to, um, really dive into my English studies or maybe take a class. Also, more time to relax, like read a book or just, you know, have some moments to myself without feeling rushed.

interview_script.question: Biggest constraint last year?
interview_script.answer: Hmm, I’d say the transition with my kids starting a new school. It was a lot to handle—new routines, new friends, making sure they’re doing okay, you know? Plus, balancing that with my own learning and adapting.

interview_script.question: How do you deal with that constraint?
interview_script.answer: Communication was key. I talked a lot with the teachers, other parents, and, um, I involved my kids in conversations about their feelings and experiences. We took it one day at a time, and having a consistent routine helped a lot too.

interview_script.question: People you feel closest to?
interview_script.answer: My family, of course, my husband and kids. And I have a couple of really close friends back in Brazil. We talk often. Here in Miami, I’ve made a few good friends through the kids’ school and our neighborhood.

interview_script.question: Describe those relationships.
interview_script.answer: They’re supportive, you know? With my husband, we’re partners in everything. My friends, they’re my go-to for advice and laughs. It’s like having a little piece of home with me in Miami.

interview_script.question: Where do you spend most of your time?
interview_script.answer: Mostly at home, I’d say. Between taking care of the house, the kids, and practicing my English, I’m here a lot. But I also try to get out to parks and local events when we can.

interview_script.question: How do you feel in those spaces?
interview_script.answer: Home is where I feel comfortable and safe, you know? It’s my space to recharge. Outside, like at parks or events, I feel, um, more connected to the community and the world around me. It’s refreshing.

interview_script.question: What makes you feel that way?
interview_script.answer: Having my family around at home and being able to unwind. Outside, it’s the interaction with people, seeing the kids play, feeling like I’m part of something bigger than just myself.

interview_script.question: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
interview_script.answer: I usually turn to my husband first. We’re a team in everything. Then, if I need more perspective, I’ll call my mom in Brazil or chat with my close friend here. They’re all great listeners and give me comfort and guidance.

interview_script.question: One tough moment in the last year?
interview_script.answer: There was a time when my son was struggling with his new school. He was finding it hard to make friends, and it broke my heart to see him sad. It was tough because I wanted to help, but I also knew he needed to work through it himself with our support.

interview_script.question: How did it affect you?
interview_script.answer: It was stressful, and I felt helpless at times, you know? It made me question if we’d made the right choices and if I was doing enough as a mom. But it also pushed me to find ways to support him better.

interview_script.question: How did you cope?
interview_script.answer: We talked a lot, both with my son and as a family, about his feelings and ideas. We also reached out to the school counselors, who were helpful. I encouraged social activities and playdates with classmates to help him build friendships. And I focused on keeping things positive at home, so he always had a safe space.

interview_script.question: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
interview_script.answer: Taking a step back, breathing, and maybe doing a short Duolingo session or listening to music helps me relax. Also, just talking to my husband or a friend helps me see things clearer and, um, not feel so alone in it.

interview_script.question: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
interview_script.answer: I hope we’re more settled here, you know, with a strong circle of friends. I want my English to be, um, much better—fluent and natural. I also want to be doing something for myself, maybe a part-time job or volunteering, giving back to the community.

interview_script.question: What do you want to be different?
interview_script.answer: I’d love to feel more integrated into the community here, more engaged beyond just school activities. And for my own learning, I want more opportunities to practice English in real conversations.

interview_script.question: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
interview_script.answer: Before Duolingo, um, I tried a few traditional methods like textbooks and CDs. But they were, you know, hard to keep up with, especially with little kids running around. I also tried some classes, but the schedule was too rigid for me. It was frustrating trying to fit those into my busy life.

interview_script.question: Most annoying part of old method?
interview_script.answer: The lack of flexibility, definitely. I mean, I couldn’t just pick it up anytime like I do with Duolingo. And it felt more like a chore than something fun, you know? It was hard to stay motivated.

interview_script.question: Time it really failed?
interview_script.answer: There was this time when I signed up for an English class, thinking it would help. But between family duties and unpredictable schedules, I missed several classes. It ended up being a waste of money and made me feel, um, really discouraged about learning.

interview_script.question: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: A friend of mine in Brazil mentioned it during a chat. She was using it to learn Spanish. She said it was really fun and easy, so I thought, why not give it a try for English?

interview_script.question: What convinced you to try it?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, the fact that it was free and I could use it on my phone was a big plus. I also liked that it was, um, designed like a game, which sounded way more fun than my old methods. And my friend swore by it, so I figured it was worth checking out.

interview_script.question: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
interview_script.answer: Sure! So, just yesterday, after breakfast, I opened Duolingo. I decided to do a lesson on food vocabulary—it's one of my favorites! The app started with a mix of translating sentences and matching words with pictures. I like how it keeps you engaged with different activities. Then I moved on to the speaking exercise, which is always a bit nerve-wracking, but it’s good practice. I love when it says 'Você é incrível!' at the end of a lesson—it makes me feel proud of myself.

interview_script.question: Most helpful part?
interview_script.answer: The bite-sized lessons! They fit into my day so easily. I can do them while waiting for, um, my kids at school or when I have a few minutes of free time. Also, the instant feedback helps me correct mistakes right away, which is great for learning.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part?
interview_script.answer: Sometimes the app can be a bit repetitive, you know? Like, I've learned a word, but it keeps showing up in lessons instead of moving on. And, um, the speech recognition isn't always perfect. It can be a bit frustrating when it doesn't get what I'm saying, especially when I know I’m saying it right!

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
interview_script.answer: I think it’s when I feel like I'm ready to jump to more complex sentences, but the app keeps giving me simpler exercises. I get it’s about mastery, but sometimes I want more challenge, you know? Also, the ads can be a bit intrusive when you’re in the middle of learning.

interview_script.question: One time that frustration showed up?
interview_script.answer: Oh, yes. There was this one time I was having a good streak, lesson after lesson, and then, boom, I got stuck on this dumb, um, simple sentence exercise that was repeated too many times. I felt like I wasn't moving forward. It made me close the app for that day.

interview_script.question: Do you use workarounds?
interview_script.answer: Yes, sometimes I do. When I feel stuck, I complement my practice with YouTube videos or podcasts for more advanced vocabulary and listening practice. It helps to mix things up a bit and keeps the learning process fresh and interesting.

interview_script.question: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
interview_script.answer: Um, more variety and context, I guess. Watching videos or listening to podcasts puts words and phrases into real-life situations, which Duolingo sometimes, um, lacks. It also helps me to hear different accents and speeds, which is great for comprehension.

interview_script.question: Worst-case scenario in this space?
interview_script.answer: For me, the worst-case would be hitting a plateau where I don’t feel any progress. That would be discouraging, because, you know, it’s important to feel you’re moving forward, especially when you put time and effort into learning.

interview_script.question: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
interview_script.answer: I hope it gives me, uh, that little boost of confidence each time I complete a lesson. I want it to challenge me just enough to keep me learning but also make me feel successful. It should, um, feel rewarding and motivate me to come back.

interview_script.question: How do you know Duolingo worked?
interview_script.answer: When I can use what I’ve learned in real conversations or understand something new, like in a TV show or an article, then I know it’s working. And also, when I see those little green checks after completing a lesson—it’s a good feeling!

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I’d love to see more interactive speaking exercises, maybe something that mimics real-life conversations more closely. It would be so helpful to practice, um, how people actually speak day-to-day.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
interview_script.answer: It would be great if language learning resources were more integrated. Like having a platform that combines, um, Duolingo's gamified approach with real-world practice, videos, podcasts—all in one place, so it’s more comprehensive.

interview_script.question: Anything important we didn't cover?
interview_script.answer: I think we covered a lot, but I’d just add that, um, using Duolingo has built my confidence in speaking English more than I ever expected. It’s really empowering to feel progress, even if it’s just a little every day.

interview_script.question: Permission to build a digital twin?
interview_script.answer: Sure, as long as it respects my privacy and helps improve language learning tools, I’m happy to help!
